NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage describes research on how small bats choose among roosts with different temperatures.

For a small bat, rest is not biologically inactive. Even while hanging still, the animal must balance energy conservation against the need to become alert quickly. A cool shelter can reduce the energy required to maintain body temperature if the bat enters torpor, a controlled state in which metabolism slows. Yet leaving torpor requires reheating muscles before flight. A warmer shelter costs more energy during rest but may shorten that delay.

Researchers studying canyon bats suspected that roost choice would change with immediate conditions rather than follow a fixed preference. They installed wooden roost boxes on the same cliff face. Dark outer panels made some boxes warm rapidly after sunrise; reflective panels kept others cooler. Sensors recorded air and wall temperatures, and harmless tags detected when individual bats entered or departed.

During mild nights, many bats selected cooler boxes before dawn. These animals remained inside well into the morning and showed body temperatures consistent with torpor. The pattern fit an energy-saving strategy: when no early activity was necessary, a cool roost allowed metabolism to remain low.

The pattern shifted after nights when researchers played brief recordings of hunting owls near the cliff. The recordings ended hours before sunrise and no predator was present at the boxes. Nevertheless, tagged bats more often entered warmer roosts. They also departed sooner when a second owl recording was played after dawn. Researchers proposed that a warmer body reduced the time required to begin controlled flight.

That interpretation required caution. The owl recordings might have changed where insects gathered, or they might have caused bats to avoid a part of the cliff rather than select temperature itself. To separate location from warmth, the team rotated dark and reflective panels among boxes every few days. Preference followed the thermal treatment more closely than box position, weakening the simple location explanation.

A second experiment added heating pads to several cool-looking boxes while leaving their exterior panels unchanged. Bats used the secretly warmed boxes at rates similar to naturally warm ones after owl recordings. This result indicated that internal temperature, not visible panel color, influenced the choice. It did not prove that rapid escape was the only benefit, but it connected the behavior more directly to thermal conditions.

Adult females carrying young did not follow the general pattern as strongly. They favored warmer boxes even without predator cues. Developing young cannot regulate temperature as effectively as adults, and repeated cooling could slow growth. The needs of offspring therefore appeared to narrow the range of acceptable choices.

Weather added another constraint. On very hot afternoons, the darkest boxes reached temperatures that could cause dangerous water loss. Bats abandoned them regardless of earlier owl recordings. A feature beneficial under one condition became costly when pushed beyond a safe range.

The study does not reduce roost choice to a single calculation. Temperature interacts with predators, reproduction, weather, and the time at which flight may be needed. What appears to be inconsistency may instead be flexible decision-making: bats shift among shelters because the biological value of warmth changes from one night to the next.

Individual history mattered as well. Bats that had occupied one box repeatedly were somewhat more likely to return to it, even when another box offered a slightly more favorable temperature. Familiarity may reduce the time spent inspecting crevices or the risk of entering an unsafe shelter. When temperature differences became large, however, thermal conditions outweighed that tendency.

The researchers did not treat box choice as identical to natural roost choice. Rock cracks vary in depth, humidity, airflow, and access routes in ways that wooden boxes cannot reproduce. The boxes allowed controlled comparisons, but observations in natural cracks were still needed to test whether the same tradeoffs operated there. Repeated seasons would also show whether individual bats preserve these preferences as their reproductive condition and experience change.
